title: String Memory Structure
concept: There is no ‘string type’ in C language. It is simply written by adding 0 to the end of the character array.

steps.title: Include stdio.h header
steps.explanation:
Standard input/output header for using `printf`.

This lesson examines how strings are stored as `char` arrays.

steps.title: Start main function
steps.explanation:
The main frame is created.

See step by step how string literals go into an array.

steps.title: Declare a string as an array of characters
steps.explanation:
`char str[] = "Code";` creates an array containing four characters plus the terminating character `\0`.

That is, the actual array size will be 5.

steps.title: String output (%s)
steps.explanation:
`%s` prints characters until it encounters `\0`.

So only the text part of `str` appears as a normal string.

steps.title: Check the total size of an array (sizeof)
steps.explanation:
`sizeof(str)` returns the total number of bytes in the array.

Since the return type is `size_t`, the output format uses `%zu`.

steps.title: Check array contents directly
steps.explanation:
If you print each column by index, you can also check the ending character value (0) at the end.

The key point is that the string ends with an invisible `\0`.

steps.title: Program exit
steps.explanation:
Exit with `return 0;`.

Key point: String literals even include the terminating character when copied into an array.

quiz.question: char buf[5] = "Hello"; Why is it dangerous?
options: It is not recognized as a string because there is no final \0 space.
quiz.explanation:
"Hello" has 5 characters, but requires 6 spaces including `\0`.
If you force it into `buf[5]`, there is no end mark, so when output, a line appears all the way to the back memory (the beginning of Buffer Overflow).

misconceptions.wrong: The length of a string can be found with `sizeof`.
misconceptions.correct: In most cases, you should use `strlen`.
misconceptions.why: `sizeof` is the overall size of the container (array), and `strlen` is the actual length of its contents (before `\0`).

keyTakeaway: In C, a string is a `char` array terminated with `0`. Always remember the `+1` field.
